events.title: Earliest Human Settlement
events.description: Archaeological evidence shows earliest human presence on Brazilian territory. The 'Luzia' skull fossil discovered in Lapa Vermelha cave, Minas Gerais, is considered one of the oldest human remains in the Americas, dating about 11000-12000 years ago. These early inhabitants likely migrated from Asia via the Bering land bridge, gradually spreading to South America. They lived hunter-gatherer lifestyles.

events.title: Rock Art Culture
events.description: Serra da Capivara National Park in Piauí, northeast Brazil, preserves extensive prehistoric rock paintings depicting hunting scenes, rituals and daily life. These paintings are among the most important prehistoric art sites in the Americas, showing complex culture and artistic expression of early inhabitants. Rock art includes human figures, animals and abstract patterns.

events.title: Pottery Culture Development
events.description: Pottery making emerged in the Amazon region, marking development of settled agricultural societies. The Santarém region pottery culture was particularly advanced, showing complex social organization. Large mounds and pottery fragments found on Marajó Island prove existence of densely populated settlements. These societies developed agricultural techniques, cultivating manioc, maize and other crops.

events.title: 1964 Military Coup
events.description: Military launched coup in Minas Gerais, overthrowing President Goulart. Coup received support from conservative politicians, business, media and US (US 'Operation Brother Sam' prepared military support for coup). Goulart refused resistance to avoid civil war, exiled to Uruguay. Military called coup 'revolution,' claiming saved Brazil from communism. Coup opened 21 years (1964-1985) military dictatorship, Brazil's darkest democratic period. Initially military promised short intervention then restore democracy, but soon established long-term dictatorship regime. 1964 coup part of US-supported Latin American right-wing military coup wave during Cold War.

events.title: Marajoara Culture Flourishing
events.description: Marajó Island at Amazon River mouth developed complex indigenous culture, building large earthen mounds (tesos) with population possibly reaching tens of thousands. They created elaborate polychrome pottery, developed complex social hierarchies and religious rituals. This culture challenged traditional views that Amazon could not support large settled civilizations. The culture flourished until European contact.

events.title: Tupi Migration and Expansion
events.description: Tupi-speaking peoples began massive migration from Amazon interior toward Atlantic coast. The Tupi (including Tupinambá, Tupinikin and other tribes) eventually controlled most of Brazil's coast. They practiced slash-and-burn agriculture, cultivating manioc, beans, squash, also hunting and fishing. Tupi language and culture profoundly influenced later Brazilian society, with many place names and words deriving from Tupi.

events.title: Pre-Colonial Indigenous Societies
events.description: Before European arrival, Brazilian territory was inhabited by an estimated 2-6 million indigenous people belonging to hundreds of different tribes and language families, mainly including Tupi-Guarani, Gê, Arawak and Carib. Coastal regions were dominated by Tupi engaging in agriculture and fishing; interior and Amazon regions included more diverse hunting-gathering and agricultural societies. Social organization ranged from small mobile groups to large villages of thousands, with complex trade networks, alliances and conflicts.

events.title: Early Exploration and Brazilwood Trade
events.description: Portugal initially showed limited interest in Brazil, focused on lucrative Indian spice trade. But Portuguese merchants began exploiting brazilwood (pau-brasil) trade, tree's red dye highly valued in Europe, giving country its name 'Brazil.' Portuguese established coastal trading posts, exchanging brazilwood, parrots and other goods with Tupi indigenous. French also began incursions, threatening Portuguese sovereignty. This prompted Portuguese crown to systematically colonize Brazil.

events.title: Cabral's Discovery of Brazil
events.description: Portuguese navigator Pedro Álvares Cabral, leading fleet to India, accidentally discovered Brazilian coast, landing at Porto Seguro in present Bahia state. Cabral claimed the land for Portugal, initially naming it 'Land of the True Cross' (Terra da Vera Cruz). Accompanying scribe Pero Vaz de Caminha wrote to Portuguese King Manuel I, detailing the new land and friendly indigenous inhabitants. This discovery changed Brazil's and entire South America's historical trajectory.

events.title: First Colonization Expedition
events.description: King João III of Portugal sent Martim Afonso de Sousa leading first official colonization expedition to Brazil, aiming to establish permanent settlements, expel French intruders, and begin organized colonization. Expedition established Brazil's first permanent settlement at São Vicente (present São Paulo state), marking beginning of systematic colonization. Sousa also introduced sugarcane cultivation, laying foundation for later sugar economy.

events.title: Hereditary Captaincies System
events.description: To promote colonization without draining royal treasury, João III divided Brazilian coast into 15 hereditary captaincies (capitanias hereditárias), granted to nobles and wealthy merchants. Captains responsible for developing territory at own expense, in exchange for extensive administrative and economic powers. But most captaincies failed due to indigenous resistance, lack of resources and mismanagement, only Pernambuco and São Vicente achieved some success. System's failure prompted crown to establish more centralized administration.

events.title: Establishment of General Government and Salvador Founded
events.description: Given hereditary captaincies' failure, Portuguese king established General Government to unify administration of Brazil colony. First governor-general Tomé de Sousa founded Salvador city in Bahia as colonial capital, first planned Brazilian city. Jesuit missionaries accompanied governor-general, beginning systematic evangelization of indigenous and establishing educational institutions. Salvador became Brazil's colonial political and economic center for over 200 years.

events.title: Sugar Boom and Plantation Economy
events.description: Sugarcane cultivation and sugar production became backbone of Brazil's colonial economy. Northeast especially Pernambuco and Bahia became main sugar-producing regions. Large sugar mills (engenhos) required massive labor, initially using indigenous slaves, but due to disease, escape and Jesuit protection, colonists turned to importing African slaves. Brazil became world's largest sugar producer, bringing enormous wealth to Portugal. Sugar economy shaped Brazil's social structure: large landowners, slaves and few free people in stratified society.

events.title: France Antarctique and French Threat
events.description: France established colony 'France Antarctique' in Rio de Janeiro Bay, led by Nicolas Durand de Villegaignon, threatening Portuguese sovereignty. French allied with local Tupinambá tribes. 1560 Portuguese governor-general Mem de Sá launched expedition, after years of fighting, finally expelled French in 1567, establishing Rio de Janeiro city on French colony's site. This victory consolidated Portuguese control over Brazilian coast.

events.title: Iberian Union Period
events.description: After Portuguese King Sebastian I died childless in Morocco battle, 1580 Spanish King Philip II inherited Portuguese throne, Portugal and Brazil entered 60 years of Spanish Habsburg rule. This made Brazil target of Spain's enemies (especially Dutch). But period also facilitated Brazil's westward expansion beyond Tordesillas Treaty line, as Spanish-Portuguese rulers more tolerant of Brazilian expansion. 1640 Portugal restored independence, João IV crowned.

events.title: Bandeirantes Expeditions
events.description: Bandeirantes (pioneers) from São Paulo organized armed expeditions deep into interior, seeking gold, gems and capturing indigenous slaves. They explored along rivers, penetrating Amazon, Central-West and southern interior, greatly expanding Portuguese-controlled territory far beyond Tordesillas Treaty limits. Bandeirantes attacked Jesuit missions (reduções) protecting indigenous, causing massive indigenous population decline. Though brutal, bandeirantes laid foundation for Brazil's current vast territory, viewed as controversial historical figures.

events.title: Dutch First Invasion of Bahia
events.description: Dutch West India Company at war with Spain invaded and briefly occupied Salvador, Brazil's colonial capital. Dutch attempted to seize lucrative sugar industry. But Portuguese-Spanish joint fleet recaptured Salvador in 1625, ending one year of Dutch rule. This began Dutch-Portuguese conflict in Brazil.

events.title: Dutch Brazil
events.description: Dutch West India Company invaded and occupied most of northeast Brazil, including Pernambuco, wealthiest sugar-producing region. 1637 Johan Maurits van Nassau-Siegen appointed Dutch Brazil governor-general, establishing modern administration in Recife, promoting religious tolerance (allowing Jews and Protestants), funding scientific and artistic expeditions, modernizing urban planning. But after Maurits left 1644, Dutch rule deteriorated. Local Portuguese, blacks and mixed residents launched uprising (Insurreição Pernambucana), after guerrilla warfare, Dutch finally surrendered and withdrew 1654. Dutch Brazil period influenced Recife urban development and Brazil's cultural diversity.

events.title: Quilombo dos Palmares
events.description: Escaped slaves established Palmares quilombo (escaped slave community) in Alagoas interior mountains, largest and longest-lasting slave resistance stronghold in Americas history. Under leaders Ganga Zumba and later Zumbi, Palmares developed into federal state with tens of thousands population, resisting Dutch and Portuguese armies for nearly century. Palmares practiced mixed African and indigenous culture, economically self-sufficient. 1694 after multiple expeditions, Portuguese army finally destroyed Palmares, Zumbi killed. Zumbi became symbol of Brazilian abolitionism and black resistance, November 20 (his death anniversary) designated Brazilian Black Consciousness Day.

events.title: Discovery of Gold
events.description: Bandeirantes discovered large gold deposits in Minas Gerais region (meaning 'General Mines'). This discovery triggered Brazil's gold rush, tens of thousands flooding from coast and Portuguese mainland to interior mining regions. Gold discovery changed Brazil's economic and demographic center, from northeast sugar regions to southeast mining areas. New towns like Ouro Preto, Mariana, Sabará rapidly rose. Portuguese crown strictly controlled gold mining and taxation.

events.title: Emboabas War
events.description: In Minas Gerais gold mining regions, violent conflict erupted between early bandeirantes from São Paulo (paulistas) and later arrivals (mainly Portuguese and northeastern Brazilians, called emboabas) competing for mining area control and rights. Conflict caused hundreds of deaths. Eventually Portuguese crown intervened, 1709 separated mining regions from São Paulo captaincy, establishing independent Minas Gerais captaincy, ending São Paulo monopoly.

events.title: Discovery of Diamonds
events.description: Diamond mines discovered in northern Minas Gerais Serro region, triggering new mining boom. Portuguese crown established strict monopoly system controlling diamond extraction and trade. Diamantina city became diamond mining center. Gold and diamonds made 18th century Portuguese crown extremely wealthy, but most wealth wasted on luxury consumption and religious buildings rather than investing in industrialization.

events.title: Treaty of Madrid
events.description: Portugal and Spain signed Treaty of Madrid, redefining South American colonial boundaries, replacing outdated Tordesillas Treaty. Treaty recognized 'uti possidetis' principle (who actually controls land owns sovereignty). This legalized Portuguese control of vast interior territories expanded by bandeirantes, establishing foundation of Brazil's modern borders. Brazilian territory greatly exceeded original treaty line, becoming South America's largest country.

events.title: Pombaline Reforms
events.description: Portuguese Prime Minister Marquis of Pombal implemented series of enlightened absolutist reforms affecting Brazil. Reforms included: expelling Jesuits (1759) and confiscating their property and missions; abolishing legal barriers to indigenous-white intermarriage; promoting indigenous assimilation; encouraging industry and trade; reforming education. Pombal also strengthened crown control over colony, limiting local elite power. These reforms modernized Brazilian administration, but also provoked conservative opposition.

events.title: Capital Moved to Rio de Janeiro
events.description: Colonial capital moved from Salvador to Rio de Janeiro, reflecting economic and political center's shift toward southern mining regions. Rio de Janeiro geographically closer to Minas Gerais gold mines and Europe, better port conditions. This change marked northeast sugar region's decline and southeast's rise, shaping modern Brazil's regional imbalance pattern.

events.title: Minas Conspiracy
events.description: Inspired by American Independence and Enlightenment ideas, Minas Gerais colonial elite plotted conspiracy (Inconfidência Mineira) against Portuguese rule. Leaders included poet Tomás Antônio Gonzaga and officer Joaquim José da Silva Xavier (nicknamed 'Tiradentes,' meaning 'tooth-puller'). They planned uprising when overdue gold tax collection occurred, to establish republic, abolish slavery. But conspiracy betrayed, leaders arrested. Most exiled, Tiradentes executed as scapegoat in 1792, hanged and quartered. Tiradentes later became martyr and national hero of Brazilian independence movement, symbolizing Brazil's earliest pursuit of freedom.

events.title: Portuguese Royal Court Moves to Brazil
events.description: When Napoleon's army invaded Portugal, Prince Regent João (later João VI) led Portuguese royal court, government and about 15000 nobles, officials under British naval protection, fleeing to Brazil. 1808 royal court arrived Rio de Janeiro, first time European monarchy established in New World. João elevated Rio de Janeiro to de facto capital of Portuguese Empire. This event completely changed Brazil's status, from colony to imperial center, greatly accelerating Brazil's cultural, economic and political development.

events.title: United Kingdom and Modernization
events.description: Prince João (becoming King João VI 1816) conducted major reforms and modernization in Brazil. He opened ports to international trade (ending Portuguese monopoly); created Bank of Brazil, Royal Press, National Library; established higher education institutions (medical, military and art academies); invited French Artistic Mission bringing neoclassical art and architecture. 1815 Brazil elevated to kingdom equal with Portugal, two formed 'United Kingdom of Portugal, Brazil and Algarves.' Rio de Janeiro became vibrant cultural and economic center. But royal court's expenses and favoritism toward Portuguese caused Brazilian native elite discontent.

events.title: Pernambuco Revolution
events.description: Northeast Brazil's Pernambuco erupted republican revolution against João VI's autocratic rule, heavy taxation and Portuguese monopoly of offices. Rebels established short-lived Pernambuco Republic, promulgating liberal constitution, declaring religious freedom and abolishing certain privileges. But revolution lacked mass support and isolated, 75 days later crushed by royal army. Leaders executed or exiled. Though failed, revolution showed republican and liberal ideas' influence in Brazil, paving way for later independence movement.

events.title: Liberal Revolution and João VI's Return to Portugal
events.description: 1820 Portugal erupted liberal revolution, constitutional assembly demanded king return to Lisbon. João VI faced dilemma: staying in Brazil might lose Portuguese throne, returning might lose Brazil. April 1821 he returned Portugal, leaving son Prince Pedro as Brazil's regent. Lisbon's new parliament attempted to reduce Brazil back to colony status, revoking its autonomy and institutions, causing Brazilian elite strong discontent. These policies directly led to Brazilian independence movement.

events.title: War of Independence
events.description: Though Brazilian independence relatively peaceful, still required military action to consolidate. Portugal still had garrisons resisting in Bahia, Maranhão, Pará, Cisplatina (present Uruguay). Brazil with British mercenary help (including Admiral Lord Thomas Cochrane), through land and sea campaigns, by end 1823 expelled all Portuguese garrisons, completely controlling territory. 1825 Portugal formally recognized Brazilian independence (Brazil paid 2 million pounds compensation).

events.title: 'I Stay' Declaration
events.description: Portuguese parliament ordered Prince Pedro return to Europe, but Brazilian elite (especially led by José Bonifácio de Andrada) petitioned him to stay. At Rio de Janeiro's Ipiranga River banks, Pedro declared 'I Stay' (Fico), refusing to return Portugal. This viewed as key turning point in Brazil's independence process, Pedro choosing to stand with Brazil, against Lisbon's commands.

events.title: Brazilian Independence
events.description: Near São Paulo at Ipiranga River banks, Prince Pedro received letters from Portugal demanding Brazil completely submit to Lisbon parliament. Angry Pedro drew sword declaring 'Independence or Death!' (Independência ou Morte!), the famous 'Cry of Ipiranga.' September 7 became Brazil's Independence Day. October 12 Pedro proclaimed Emperor Pedro I of Brazil, establishing Brazilian Empire. Unlike Spanish America's bloody independence wars, Brazilian independence relatively peaceful, led by Portuguese royal family member, maintaining monarchical system.

events.title: First Constitution
events.description: Brazilian Empire promulgated first constitution, establishing constitutional monarchy. Constitution stipulated four-power separation (executive, legislative, judicial and 'moderating power,' moderating power exercised by emperor to balance other powers), establishing bicameral parliament (Senate and Chamber of Deputies). Constitution granted emperor extensive powers, including appointing senators, vetoing legislation and dissolving parliament. Constitution also established Catholicism as state religion (but allowed other religions private worship), and limited suffrage to propertied citizens. This constitution lasted until 1889 republic, one of Latin America's most enduring constitutions.

events.title: Confederation of the Equator Uprising
events.description: Northeast Brazil (Pernambuco, Ceará, Paraíba, Rio Grande do Norte) erupted republican and separatist uprising against Pedro I's authoritarianism and 1824 constitution's centralization. Rebels declared establishing 'Confederation of the Equator,' advocating republicanism and local autonomy. But uprising poorly organized, lacked mass support, 1825 crushed by imperial army. Leaders executed, but uprising reflected regional discontent with centralization and monarchy, tension persisting throughout imperial period.

events.title: Cisplatine War
events.description: Argentina-supported Cisplatine province (present Uruguay) independence movement triggered Brazil-Argentina war. War extremely costly, neither side achieving decisive victory. 1828 under British mediation signed peace treaty, Cisplatina became independent Oriental Republic of Uruguay, as buffer state between Brazil and Argentina. War's failure weakened Pedro I's prestige, increased fiscal burden, exacerbated domestic political crisis.

events.title: Pedro I's Abdication
events.description: Due to Cisplatine War failure, economic difficulties, authoritarian tendencies and Portuguese succession crisis (his daughter Maria II's throne in Portugal usurped), Pedro I faced widespread domestic opposition. Rio de Janeiro erupted street protests, military defected. April 7 1831 Pedro I abdicated, passing throne to five-year-old son Pedro II, then returned Europe to fight for daughter's Portuguese throne. Abdication marked Brazilian political power shift from emperor to parliamentary elite.

events.title: Regency Period
events.description: Pedro II young, Brazil entered Regency Period, ruled by regency council and later individual regents. This one of most turbulent periods in Brazilian history, full of political instability, regional rebellions and separatist movements. Central government weak, provinces demanding greater autonomy. Period erupted multiple massive uprisings: Rio Grande do Sul's Farroupilha Revolution, Pará's Cabanagem Rebellion, Bahia's Sabinada, Maranhão's Balaiada. Regency period's chaos prompted elite to decide prematurely ending regency, letting Pedro II assume power early.

events.title: Farroupilha Revolution
events.description: Rio Grande do Sul province erupted separatist revolution against central government demanding regional autonomy. Rebels declared establishing 'Riograndense Republic' (República Rio-Grandense), later expanded to Santa Catarina establishing 'Juliana Republic.' This Brazil's longest civil war, lasting ten years, causing thousands deaths. Rebels received Argentina and Uruguay support. 1845 under Luís Alves de Lima e Silva (Duke of Caxias) leadership, imperial army through military action and negotiation reached reconciliation, granting rebels amnesty and local certain autonomy. Caxias thus hailed as 'Peacemaker.'

events.title: Pedro II's Reign
events.description: Pedro II ruled nearly half century, one of most stable and prosperous periods in Brazilian history. Emperor scholar and intellectual, passionate about science, education and culture, patronizing arts and educational institutions. He practiced relatively enlightened rule, respecting constitution and parliament, tolerating opposition voices. Two-party system (Liberal and Conservative) alternated power, though differences slight. Economy dependent on coffee exports and slave labor. Pedro II personally opposed slavery, but due to political resistance acted slowly. His rule solidified Brazilian unity, avoiding Spanish America's fragmentation and warlordism, but by late 19th century, republicanism and abolitionist movement gradually undermined Empire's foundation.

events.title: Pedro II's Early Majority
events.description: Facing Regency period chaos and separatist threats, Brazilian elite decided to make 14-year-old Pedro II assume power early, though constitution stipulated 18 years old majority. This coup called 'Majority Coup' (Golpe da Maioridade). Parliament passed law declaring Pedro II adult and crowned as emperor. Pedro II's assumption marked Empire entering stable period, he became symbol of stability and unity, ruling Brazil nearly 50 years.

events.title: Prohibition of Slave Trade
events.description: Under British pressure (Britain through Aberdeen Act unilaterally authorized Royal Navy to intercept slave ships), Brazil promulgated Eusébio de Queirós Law, formally prohibiting Atlantic slave trade. Though enforcement initially lax, by mid-1850s, trans-Atlantic slave trade actually stopped. This forced Brazilian economy to seek alternative labor, stimulating European immigration and internal slave trade (from Northeast to Southeast coffee regions). This first step in Brazil's abolition process, but slavery itself persisted nearly 40 years.

events.title: Coffee Boom
events.description: Coffee replaced sugar as Brazil's most important export commodity, dominating economy until early 20th century. São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro and Minas Gerais states became main coffee-producing regions. Coffee plantations (fazendas) initially used slave labor, after abolition turned to European immigrants (especially Italians). Coffee wealth created powerful coffee oligarchy (coffee barons), dominating Brazilian politics and economy. Coffee export revenue funded infrastructure construction (railways, ports) and urbanization. 'Coffee with Milk' politics (São Paulo coffee and Minas Gerais dairy alliance) dominated First Republic. Brazil became world's largest coffee producer, monopolizing global market.

events.title: Platine War
events.description: Brazil allied with Uruguay and Argentine anti-Rosas faction against Argentine dictator Juan Manuel de Rosas. Brazil feared Rosas expansionism threatening Brazil's southern borders. 1852 allied army defeated Rosas at Battle of Caseros, he forced into exile. This victory established Brazil's influence in La Plata region, but also laid groundwork for later conflict with Paraguay.

events.title: Paraguayan War
events.description: Also called War of Triple Alliance, Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay alliance against Paraguayan dictator Francisco Solano López. This South America's bloodiest war, Paraguay losing about 60-70% population. War caused by power struggle in La Plata region and Paraguayan expansionism. Brazil committed vast resources, mobilizing over 200000 troops (including slaves, promised freedom after service). Duke of Caxias led Brazilian army to victory. 1870 López killed, war ended. War strengthened Brazilian army's political influence, veteran officers became abolitionism and republican movement supporters. War's enormous cost also weakened Empire finances.

events.title: Free Womb Law
events.description: With Pedro II support, Empire promulgated Free Womb Law (Lei do Ventre Livre), declaring children born to slaves after September 28 1871 free (though required serving master until 21). This important step in Brazil's abolition process, but too gradual, abolitionist movement considered insufficient. Law ensured eventual abolition, but time too long, showing slaveholder forces still powerful.

events.title: Abolitionist Movement Peak
events.description: 1880s abolitionist movement reached peak, lawyers like Luís Gama (himself escaped slave) and Joaquim Nabuco leading abolitionists' propaganda, legal battles and parliamentary activities. André Rebouças, José do Patrocínio and other black and mixed intellectuals also played important roles. Abolitionist movement gained urban middle class, students, officers and Princess Isabel (Pedro II's daughter) support. Multiple provinces unilaterally declared abolition (Ceará and Amazonas 1884). Slaves massively escaping, plantation owners finding increasingly difficult maintaining system.

events.title: Sexagenarian Law
events.description: Promulgated Saraiva-Cotegipe Law (Lei dos Sexagenários), freeing slaves over 60. But law effect limited and ridiculed as hypocritical, because most slaves in harsh conditions didn't live to 60, and elderly slaves had limited economic value to masters. But law reflected slavery system gradually disintegrating, pressure mounting.

events.title: Golden Law and Abolition of Slavery
events.description: While Pedro II convalescing in Europe, regent Princess Isabel signed Golden Law (Lei Áurea), unconditionally abolishing Brazilian slavery, freeing about 700000 slaves. Brazil became last country in Western Hemisphere to abolish slavery. Abolition celebrated joyously in cities, but gave former slaves no land or compensation, nor slaveholders compensation. Coffee plantation owners who lost slaves (especially São Paulo's) turned to support republican movement, retaliating against Empire. Abolition justice and moral victory, but lack supporting measures led former slaves into poverty and marginalization, racial inequality persisting today.

events.title: Sword Republic
events.description: Republic's initial period ruled by military (Marshal Fonseca 1889-1891, Marshal Peixoto 1891-1894), called 'Sword Republic.' 1891 promulgated new federal republican constitution, establishing presidential system, three-power separation, federalism, abolishing monarchy, hereditary nobility and state religion status. But initial period politically turbulent: Fonseca attempted establishing dictatorship forced to resign; Naval Revolt (1893-1894) against government; Rio Grande do Sul's Federalist Revolution (1893-1895). This period filled with authoritarianism and political instability, but eventually 1894 transferred power to civilian president Prudente de Morais, opening 'Coffee with Milk' republic.

events.title: Republican Coup and Empire's End
events.description: Military coup led by Marshal Deodoro da Fonseca overthrew Pedro II, declaring republic. Coup almost bloodless, emperor then at Petrópolis summer palace. Coup causes included: coffee oligarchy lost Empire support after abolition; military discontent after post-Paraguayan War friction with government; republican and positivist ideas spreading among young officers and urban elite; church-state conflicts. Pedro II refused resistance to avoid civil war, exiled to Europe. Empire peacefully ended, opening republican era. Pedro II died in exile 1891, deeply loved by Brazilian people, remembered as wise monarch.

events.title: First Republic and Coffee with Milk Politics
events.description: Called 'Old Republic,' characterized by coffee oligarchy rule and 'Coffee with Milk' politics—São Paulo (coffee) and Minas Gerais (dairy and politics) alternating providing presidents, monopolizing federal power. Local politics controlled by 'colonels' (coronéis, local oligarchs) through patronage system. Electoral fraud widespread, suffrage limited to literate males (excluding most population). Economy dependent on coffee exports, government manipulating exchange rates and coffee prices supporting plantation owners. This period some economic growth and immigration wave (especially Italian, Portuguese, Spanish, Japanese), but political corruption, serious social inequality, urban workers and emerging middle class excluded from power.

events.title: Canudos War
events.description: Bahia interior poor peasants led by religious leader Antônio Conselheiro, established millenarian community at Canudos, practicing collectivism and refusing republic. Government viewed it as monarchist restoration and threat. After four military expeditions, 1897 Canudos completely destroyed, thousands killed. This massacre shocked Brazilian society, writer Euclides da Cunha's 'Os Sertões' (Rebellion in the Backlands) documented tragedy, revealing republic's gulf with rural poor, becoming Brazilian literature classic. Canudos War reflected republic failed addressing social inequality and rural poverty.

events.title: Vaccine Revolt
events.description: Rio de Janeiro erupted popular uprising against government mandatory smallpox vaccination policy. Mayor Pereira Passos and hygienist Oswaldo Cruz promoted radical urban renovation and public health campaign, demolishing slums, forcing vaccination. Poor considered this authoritarian and privacy invasion, plus disease and vaccine misunderstandings, erupted violent protests. Army suppressed uprising, but government forced to suspend mandatory vaccination. Though public health measures long-term beneficial (eliminating yellow fever, smallpox), revolt reflected government disconnect with ordinary people and modernization's coercive nature.

events.title: Sailor's Revolt
events.description: Navy's black sailors led by João Cândido Felisberto (called 'Black Admiral') launched uprising protesting navy's widespread corporal punishment (whipping) and racial discrimination. Rebels controlled four battleships, threatened bombarding Rio de Janeiro, demanding ending corporal punishment. Government forced to agree reforms and amnesty rebels. But shortly after government reneged, imprisoning and expelling many rebels. João Cândido imprisoned, though eventually released, suffered cruel treatment. Sailor's Revolt highlighted racial discrimination and military abuse, João Cândido became symbol of black rights.

events.title: São Paulo General Strike
events.description: Influenced by Russian Revolution and European labor movement, São Paulo erupted Brazil's first massive general strike, about 70000 workers participating. Strike led by anarchists and socialists, demanding reduced work hours, higher wages, improved working conditions, child labor prohibition. Government suppressed strike, but forced to make some concessions. This strike marked Brazilian labor movement's rise, challenging oligarchic rule. Immigrant (especially Italian) workers brought anarchist and socialist ideas to Brazil, shaping early labor movement.

events.title: Modern Art Week
events.description: February at São Paulo Municipal Theater held Modern Art Week, milestone in Brazilian cultural history. Writers, poets, artists and musicians (including Mário de Andrade, Oswald de Andrade, Anita Malfatti, Villa-Lobos) showcased modernist works, breaking academic traditions, fusing European avant-garde art and Brazilian native elements. Event provoked controversy and ridicule, but launched Brazilian modernist movement, seeking authentic Brazilian cultural identity, embracing mixed culture and folk traditions. Modernism profoundly influenced 20th century Brazilian culture and arts.

events.title: Copacabana Fort Revolt
events.description: Young officers (called 'lieutenants' tenentes) at Rio de Janeiro Copacabana Fort launched uprising against Old Republic's corruption and electoral fraud. Uprising quickly suppressed, but symbolically, 18 young officers launched suicidal charge on beach toward government troops, only two survived. This uprising opened 'Lieutenantism' movement, young reformist officers demanding moralizing politics, social reform and modernization. Lieutenant movement organized multiple uprisings in 1920s, paving way for 1930 Revolution.

events.title: Prestes Column
events.description: Led by Captain Luís Carlos Prestes, about 1500 rebels (Lieutenant movement members) formed column, conducting three-year 25000km guerrilla march in Brazilian interior, propagandizing reform and opposing oligarchic rule. Column evaded government army pursuit, crossing 12 states, attracting international attention. Though not overthrowing government, column highlighted Old Republic's fragility and interior poverty problems. Prestes became legendary figure, called 'Knight of Hope,' later became Communist Party leader. Column eventually exiled to Bolivia.

events.title: Coffee Crisis and 1930 Revolution Background
events.description: 1929 Wall Street crash and Great Depression devastated Brazilian coffee economy, coffee prices plummeted, massive unemployment and bankruptcy. Economic crisis exposed 'Coffee with Milk' oligarchic politics' fragility. 1930 presidential election, ruling group broke agreement, São Paulo's Júlio Prestes elected instead of Minas Gerais candidate. Minas Gerais, Rio Grande do Sul and Paraíba elite united supporting opposition candidate Getúlio Vargas. After Vargas defeated, his vice-presidential candidate João Pessoa assassinated, becoming revolution's spark.

events.title: Vargas Era
events.description: Getúlio Vargas rule period divided into phases: Provisional Government (1930-1934), Constitutional Government (1934-1937) and Estado Novo dictatorship (1937-1945). Vargas promoted state modernization and industrialization, established state enterprises (Petrobras oil company predecessor), steel mills, hydroelectric plants. Implemented labor legislation (minimum wage, 8-hour workday, paid vacation, pensions), establishing state-urban worker populist alliance. Suppressed Communists and Fascists. Promoted cultural nationalism, using samba and football to shape national identity. Established powerful centralized state, weakening local oligarchs. Vargas policies mixed blessings: promoting development and social security, but suppressing democracy and freedom. He 20th century Brazil's most important and controversial political figure.

events.title: 1930 Revolution
events.description: Rio Grande do Sul and Minas Gerais launched military uprising, Lieutenant movement officers supported. Rebels advanced rapidly, Rio de Janeiro military coup deposed President Prestes. October 31 Getúlio Vargas entered Rio de Janeiro, becoming provisional government head. 1930 Revolution ended First Republic and coffee oligarchy rule, opening Brazil's modernization and state interventionism new era. Vargas ruled Brazil continuously 15 years (1930-1945), then again elected (1951-1954), profoundly shaping modern Brazil.

events.title: Constitutionalist Revolution of São Paulo
events.description: São Paulo state launched armed uprising against Vargas dictatorship demanding constitution. This one of Brazil's largest civil wars, mobilizing tens of thousands, São Paulo citizens donating gold and supplies supporting war. But São Paulo isolated, other states didn't join, three months later uprising crushed by federal army. Though military defeat, uprising forced Vargas to promise constitution. 1933 convened constituent assembly, 1934 promulgated new constitution. July 9 (uprising day) became São Paulo state official holiday. This event shaped São Paulo's regional identity and resistance tradition against centralization.

events.title: Communist Uprising
events.description: Under Luís Carlos Prestes-led Brazilian Communist Party and Comintern planning, northeast Brazil (Natal, Recife) and Rio de Janeiro's left-wing officers launched uprising, attempting establish people's government. Uprising poorly organized, quickly suppressed. Vargas used uprising as pretext, implementing state of emergency, suppressing left-wing and liberal opposition, arresting thousands including Prestes and his wife (German Communist Olga Benário, later extradited to Nazis and died in concentration camp). Uprising provided political pretext for Vargas 1937 dictatorship establishment.

events.title: Estado Novo Dictatorship
events.description: 1937 presidential election eve, Vargas launched self-coup (autogolpe), dissolving Congress, abolishing 1934 constitution, declaring 'Estado Novo' (New State) dictatorship. New constitution granted president dictatorial powers, banned political parties, strictly censored media. Estado Novo influenced by European fascism (especially Portugal's Salazar regime), emphasizing nationalism, state economic intervention, corporatism. Vargas through political police (DOPS) and propaganda agency (DIP) controlled society. But he also promoted industrialization, labor rights and state-building, forming unique authoritarian populist model.

events.title: Brazil in World War II
events.description: After initial neutrality, Brazil under US pressure and German submarine attacks on Brazilian ships, 1942 declared war on Axis. Brazil only Latin American country sending ground troops to European theater. Brazilian Expeditionary Force (FEB, about 25000) fought alongside Allies in Italian campaign, participating in battles like Monte Cassino. Brazilian Air Force also participated. Participation strengthened Brazil-US relations, receiving US economic and military aid, promoting industrialization (especially Volta Redonda steel mill). Returning veterans questioned fighting for democracy yet living under dictatorship, laying groundwork for Vargas 1945 downfall.

events.title: Vargas Ousted and Democratization
events.description: After WWII democratization wave, domestic anti-dictatorship pressure, military discontent and Vargas attempting manipulate succession triggered crisis. October 29 1945 military launched coup, forcing Vargas resignation. Ended 15 years Vargas Era. Brazil entered democratic period (called Second Republic or Democratic Experiment), restoring political parties, free speech and presidential elections. Former Army Minister Enrico Gaspar Dutra elected president. 1946 promulgated democratic constitution. But Vargas maintained enormous influence, as senator and labor movement leader, 1950 re-elected president.

events.title: Second Republic Democratic Period
events.description: Brazil experienced relatively democratic period, with competitive elections, multiparty system, free speech and political debate. Major parties included Social Democratic Party (PSD), Brazilian Labor Party (PTB, Vargasist) and National Democratic Union (UDN, conservative). This period rapid economic growth, accelerating industrialization, expanding urbanization. But political instability, populism, inflation, Cold War ideological confrontation (left-right polarization) and social unrest persisted. Military intervened in politics multiple times. Eventually 1964 military coup ended democratic experiment. Though flawed, this period important democratic practice for Brazil.

events.title: First Brazilian World Cup
events.description: Brazil hosted 4th World Cup, building Maracanã Stadium in Rio de Janeiro (then world's largest). In final Brazil faced Uruguay at home, widely favored. But Uruguay upset Brazil 2-1, causing 'Maracanaço' (Maracanã Blow), becoming Brazil's greatest sports trauma. But this World Cup elevated Brazil's international image, consolidating football as national passion and identity symbol. Brazil later won World Cup five times (1958, 1962, 1970, 1994, 2002), becoming football kingdom.

events.title: Vargas Second Term
events.description: 1950 Vargas returned presidency through democratic election, winning with populist and nationalist platform. He promoted economic nationalism, establishing state oil monopoly company Petrobras, slogan 'The oil is ours' gained mass support. Attempted raising minimum wage, gaining worker support but causing conservative opposition. But term full of crises: economic difficulties, inflation, political confrontation, right-wing and US (Cold War context suspecting Vargas communist tendencies) hostility, corruption scandals. August 1954 conservatives and military demanded his resignation.

events.title: Vargas Suicide
events.description: Facing military ultimatum demanding resignation, Vargas committed suicide in presidential palace. He left emotional suicide letter, accusing domestic and foreign enemies' conspiracy, portraying himself as people's defender and elite conspiracy victim, ending with 'I leave life to enter history.' Suicide shocked Brazil, triggering nationwide mourning and riots against conservatives. Vargas became martyr for nationalism and populism. His death and letter became most dramatic moment in Brazilian political history, consolidating his legendary status as 'Father of the Poor,' influencing Brazilian politics for decades.

events.title: Kubitschek Presidency and Developmentalism
events.description: Juscelino Kubitschek elected president, promoting ambitious development plan '50 years progress in 5.' Implemented massive infrastructure and industrial projects, attracting foreign investment, establishing auto industry (Volkswagen, Ford, GM entered Brazil). Most famous deciding building new capital Brasília. Kubitschek period Brazil economy grew over 7% annually, industrialization rapidly advancing, optimism prevailing. But development through massive foreign debt and deficit financing, laying seeds for later economic crisis, accelerating inflation. Kubitschek remembered as charismatic builder president, representing Brazil's optimistic modernization period.

events.title: Brasília Inaugurated
events.description: New capital Brasília officially inaugurated, capital moved from Rio de Janeiro to interior Central-West plateau. This Kubitschek president's boldest project, symbolizing Brazil's modernization and interior development. City designed by architect Oscar Niemeyer and urban planner Lúcio Costa, adopting modernist and futurist style, from air looks like airplane. Brasília became 20th century urban planning and architecture masterpiece, 1987 listed UNESCO World Heritage (youngest heritage city). Capital move promoted interior development, but enormous cost exacerbated fiscal problems. Brasília became symbol of Brazilian ambition and modernity, though its utopian urban planning also criticized for lacking humanity.

events.title: Political Crisis and Goulart Period
events.description: 1961 Jânio Quadros elected president, but only seven months in office dramatically resigned. Vice President João Goulart (Vargasist, left-wing) succeeded, but military and conservatives opposed. After political compromise, Goulart assumed office under parliamentary system (limiting powers). 1963 referendum restored presidential system. Goulart promoted radical reforms (land reform, nationalization, worker rights), proposing 'Basic Reforms' platform. His policies and alliances with left-wing unions, students, Communists caused conservative, business, landlord and military fear, viewing him as communist threat. Cold War context, US (Kennedy and Johnson administrations) plotted against Goulart. Early 1964 political polarization reached peak, military coup overthrew Goulart.

events.title: Military Dictatorship Period
events.description: Brazil experienced 21 years military dictatorship, five generals serving as presidents (Castelo Branco, Costa e Silva, Médici, Geisel, Figueiredo). Regime characteristics included: suppressing political freedom, banning opposition parties (only allowed two controlled parties), censoring media, persecuting dissidents, torture, disappearances, exile. Simultaneously promoted economic development and infrastructure construction ('Brazilian Miracle'). Dictatorship divided into repression period (1968-1974, most brutal) and slow opening period (1974-1985). Hundreds killed or disappeared, thousands tortured. But regime also had some popular support (due to economic growth) and retained institutional structures (Congress, judiciary, though weakened). 1985 military finally transferred power, ending dictatorship, Brazil transitioning to democracy.

events.title: Institutional Act No. 5 and Repression Peak
events.description: Responding to intensifying student protests, worker strikes and armed left-wing guerrillas, military government issued Institutional Act No. 5 (AI-5), granting president dictatorial powers: closing Congress, abolishing habeas corpus, censoring media, stripping political rights, arresting without trial. This marked dictatorship's darkest period beginning. Political police (DOI-CODI) systematically used torture interrogating leftists. Thousands arrested, hundreds killed or disappeared, thousands exiled. Culture and universities subjected to strict censorship. AI-5 remained effective until 1978, symbolizing Brazil's dictatorship terror years.

events.title: Brazilian Miracle
events.description: Under President Médici leadership (1969-1974), Brazil experienced 'Economic Miracle,' GDP growing over 10% annually. Through foreign loans, large infrastructure projects (especially Trans-Amazonian Highway, Itaipu Dam), attracting multinationals, export growth achieved rapid development. Government used nationalist slogans ('Brazil, love it or leave it') and 1970 World Cup victory shaping popular support. Brazil became Latin America's largest economy. But growth unequal, wealth gap widened, development financed through massive foreign debt, laying groundwork for 1980s debt crisis. 'Miracle' also coexisted with same period's harshest repression, forming dictatorship's contradictory legacy.

events.title: Brazil Third World Cup Victory
events.description: Brazilian national team won Mexico World Cup, featuring legendary players Pelé, Jairzinho, Tostão, Rivelino, considered one of greatest teams in history. Final 4-1 defeated Italy, Pelé scored iconic header. This Brazil's third World Cup victory, permanently retained Jules Rimet Trophy. Military government used victory propagandizing nationalism and regime legitimacy. But victory also genuine moment of national joy and pride, football again proved core of Brazilian national identity. 1970 team's elegant and creative football became 'beautiful game' (jogo bonito) symbol.

events.title: Slow, Gradual, Safe Opening
events.description: President Geisel (1974-1979) initiated political opening (abertura) process, goal 'slow, gradual, safe' transition to democracy. Relaxed censorship, allowed more political debate, reduced torture (but not completely stopped). 1979 President Figueiredo continued opening, issued amnesty law, allowed exiles return, restored multiparty system. But opening resisted by military hardliners, right-wing terrorism occurred (like 1981 Rio Centro bombing). 1982 restored direct gubernatorial elections, opposition won major states. Economic crisis (debt, inflation, recession) weakened military legitimacy. 1984 'Direct Elections Now' movement demanded direct presidential elections. Though amendment failed, 1985 indirect election opposition candidate Tancredo Neves elected, ending military rule.

events.title: Amnesty Law
events.description: Military government issued amnesty law, pardoning political crimes, allowing exiled leftists and dissidents return to Brazil. But law also amnestied military and security forces' torture and murder crimes. This 'mutual amnesty' always controversial, criticized as impunity, obstructing justice. Until today, Brazil still debating whether should prosecute dictatorship period human rights violators. But amnesty also key step in democratization process, allowing political reconciliation and left's return to political stage. Many exiles (including later president Dilma Rousseff) returned after amnesty.

events.title: Direct Elections Now Movement
events.description: One of Brazil's largest mass movements, millions held rallies in cities nationwide, demanding restoring direct presidential elections (Diretas Já!). Movement crossed social classes, including workers, students, middle class, intellectuals, artists. Rio and São Paulo held million-person marches. Congressman Dante de Oliveira proposed direct election constitutional amendment. But military and conservatives manipulated, April 1984 amendment failed in Congress to reach two-thirds majority (298 votes in favor, few votes short). Though failed, movement showed democratic forces powerful, accelerating military withdrawal. 1985 through Electoral College indirect election produced civilian president, 1989 restored direct presidential elections. Direct Elections Now movement iconic moment of Brazilian civil society awakening.

events.title: Democratic Transition and Neves-Sarney Election
events.description: January 1985 Electoral College election, opposition alliance candidate Tancredo Neves defeated military-supported candidate, becoming first civilian elected president in 21 years (though through indirect election). Nation joyously celebrated dictatorship ending. But tragedy occurred: night before inauguration Neves hospitalized, March 15 Vice President José Sarney acted as president, Neves died April 21 (Brasília inauguration 25th anniversary), never inaugurated. Sarney became transition president. This marked 'New Republic' beginning, Brazil returned to democracy. But transition was 'negotiated transition' (pacto), military received amnesty and retained influence, many old elites retained power, genuine democratic consolidation required more years.

events.title: New Constitution
events.description: Constituent Assembly after two years debate, promulgated Brazil's seventh constitution (current constitution), called 'Citizens' Constitution.' Constitution detailed citizens' rights, social rights (health, education, labor rights), environmental protection, indigenous rights, restored direct presidential elections, strengthened Congress and judiciary, established federalism, prohibited torture and racism. Constitution reflected post-democratization consensus, protecting human rights and social welfare. But also criticized for too detailed and difficult to amend (requiring three-fifths majority two votes). 1988 Constitution democratic consolidation cornerstone, though amended many times, remains foundation of Brazil's legal and political order.

events.title: First Direct Presidential Election
events.description: 1989 held first direct presidential election since 1960, marking complete democratic restoration. Campaign intense, two-round voting. Left-wing Workers' Party (PT) candidate Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (Lula) represented workers and poor, facing young, wealthy, charismatic conservative Fernando Collor de Mello. Collor won with anti-corruption and modernization platform, receiving media (especially TV giant Globo) and elite support. Campaign reflected Brazilian social divisions: traditional elite vs emerging left, wealthy Southeast vs poor Northeast, conservatives vs reformers. Lula's strong performance showed left's rise, he later won 2002 election.

events.title: Collor Presidency and Impeachment
events.description: Collor promoted neoliberal reforms: opening economy, privatization, cutting tariffs, fighting inflation (confiscating savings accounts, causing widespread discontent). But government riddled with corruption. 1992 Collor's brother exposed president's corruption network with businessman Paulo César Farias. Congressional investigation committee found evidence. Nation erupted in massive protests, student 'painted faces' (caras-pintadas) movement demanding impeachment. September 1992 Chamber overwhelmingly voted impeachment, Collor suspended, Vice President Itamar Franco succeeded. December Senate tried Collor, he resigned before trial, but still sentenced eight years banned from holding public office. This Brazilian democracy's test and victory: constitutional procedures and popular pressure successfully removed corrupt president.

events.title: Real Plan and Economic Stabilization
events.description: Finance Minister Fernando Henrique Cardoso led implementing Real Plan (Plano Real), successfully controlling hyperinflation plaguing Brazil for decades. Plan introduced new currency Real, pegged to dollar, implementing fiscal discipline and monetary reform. Inflation dropped from annual rate thousands of percent to single digits, economy stabilized, people's purchasing power restored. Real Plan's success enabled Cardoso to easily win 1994 presidential election. Economic stabilization viewed as one of most important achievements in Brazil's modern history, laying foundation for later economic growth and social progress.

events.title: Brazil Fourth World Cup Victory
events.description: At World Cup held in USA, Brazil defeated Italy in penalty shootout winning championship, Brazil's fourth World Cup title, first in 24 years. Romário received Golden Ball, Bebeto and Dunga also key players. Victory restored Brazilian football confidence (failed to win 1982 and 1986, 1990 performed poorly). But 1994 team more pragmatic than elegant, drawing some criticism. Regardless, victory brought nationwide celebration, consolidating football as core of Brazilian identity and pride.

events.title: Cardoso Era
events.description: Sociologist Fernando Henrique Cardoso served two presidential terms (1995-2002), promoting neoliberal reforms: privatizing state enterprises (Vale, telecommunications), opening markets, fiscal responsibility, social safety nets (like Bolsa Escola). Constitutional amendment allowed re-election (he re-elected 1998). Economy stable but slow growth, high unemployment. 1999 currency crisis forced Real devaluation, introducing floating exchange rate. Cardoso also promoted educational expansion, land reform (limited) and acknowledging racial inequality. But neoliberal policies drew leftist criticism, social inequality persisted. Cardoso laid macroeconomic stability foundation for Lula government's success.

events.title: Lula Elected President
events.description: After three defeats (1989, 1994, 1998), Workers' Party (PT) candidate Lula won presidency in fourth attempt, defeating ruling party candidate José Serra. Lula's victory milestone in Brazilian history: first working-class origin, from poor Northeast, only elementary education president. His election represented Brazilian left and poor's rise, breaking traditional elite monopoly on power. Lula promised social change but guaranteed economic stability ('Give Lula a chance'), calming market and middle class fears. His inauguration marked Brazil's new political and social era, called 'Lula Moment.'

events.title: Brazil Fifth World Cup Victory
events.description: At Korea-Japan World Cup, Brazil with '3Rs' combination (Ronaldo, Ronaldinho, Rivaldo) won championship, final 2-0 defeated Germany. Ronaldo scored two goals, winning Golden Boot with 8 goals, proving strong comeback from injury. This Brazil's fifth World Cup title, consolidating its status as most successful national team in football history. Victory brought nationwide carnival, coinciding with Lula's election and Brazil's economic social transformation eve, symbolizing Brazil's optimism and rising moment.

events.title: Lula Era
events.description: Lula served two presidential terms (2003-2010), widely considered one of Brazil's most successful presidents. He implemented expansive social programs (especially Bolsa Família family allowance, benefiting tens of millions poor families), raised minimum wage, created jobs, expanded university education. Simultaneously maintained macroeconomic stability and fiscal responsibility, gaining market confidence. Commodity prices soaring (soybeans, iron ore, oil) drove economic boom. About 30 million Brazilians lifted from poverty, middle class expanded, inequality reduced. Lula became globally respected leader, elevating Brazil's international status (BRICS). But government also involved corruption scandals (mensalão monthly allowance scandal), Lula ultimately left office with 87% approval rating, called 'Brazil's most popular president.'

events.title: Brazil Awarded 2014 World Cup and 2016 Olympics Hosting
events.description: FIFA announced Brazil hosting 2014 World Cup (again since 1950), 2009 IOC chose Rio de Janeiro hosting 2016 Summer Olympics (South America's first). These hosting rights viewed as symbol of Brazil's rise as global power, international community's recognition of Brazil's economy and stability. But later events showed: mega-events' enormous costs, corruption, stadium waste and social protests (2013 protests partly triggered by transport fee increases and World Cup spending). But hosting also brought Brazil infrastructure improvements and international attention.

events.title: Dilma Rousseff Presidency
events.description: Lula's successor, former dictatorship guerrilla and Energy Minister Dilma Rousseff elected president (2010, re-elected 2014), becoming Brazil's first female president. First term continued Lula policies, but faced economic slowdown, inflation pressures. 2013 massive protests (initially due to bus fare increases, expanded to oppose corruption, public service quality, World Cup spending) shocked government. 2014 barely re-elected. Second term severe economic recession (GDP contracting, unemployment rising), 'Operation Car Wash' (Lava Jato) anti-corruption investigation exposed Petrobras massive corruption network, implicating political and business elite (including PT members). Dilma's approval rating plummeted.

events.title: Brazil World Cup and 'Mineiraço'
events.description: Brazil hosted World Cup, expecting home victory for sixth championship. But semifinal, Brazil 1-7 humiliatingly defeated by Germany (Mineirão Stadium), Brazil's most shameful football defeat, called 'Mineiraço,' comparable to 1950 Maracanazo. Players and people heartbroken. Third-place match lost 0-3 to Netherlands. Defeat became national trauma, also reflected Brazilian society's deeper anxieties during World Cup (economic, political, social problems). But World Cup organization successful, stadiums and events received praise.

events.title: Dilma Rousseff Impeachment
events.description: Facing economic crisis, corruption scandals and massive protests, opposition launched impeachment proceedings in Congress, accusing Dilma 'fiscal responsibility crimes' (manipulating budget, though previous governments had similar practices). May 2016 Chamber voted impeachment, Dilma suspended. August Senate voted 61-20 to remove her, Vice President Michel Temer succeeded completing term. Impeachment highly controversial: supporters claimed upholding constitution, opponents called it 'soft coup' (golpe) by conservative elite overthrowing elected left-wing president. Impeachment deepened Brazilian political polarization, weakened democratic institutions, opening politically unstable period.

events.title: Rio Olympics
events.description: Rio de Janeiro hosted Summer Olympics, South America's first. Opening ceremony showcased Brazilian cultural diversity and environmental issues. Brazil won 19 medals, including first gold medal (men's football, Neymar leading). But Olympics also faced problems: Zika virus concerns, political crisis (Dilma just removed), stadium delays, security issues. After Olympics many stadiums idle, Rio fiscal crisis deepened. Nevertheless, Olympics basically successfully held, bringing Brazil proud moments, though far from expected 'Brazil Moment' vision.

events.title: Temer Presidency and Reforms
events.description: Michel Temer completed Dilma's term, promoting controversial reforms: labor law reform (flexibility), spending cap (freezing social spending growth 20 years), attempting pension reform (unsuccessful). Reforms called necessary measures to stabilize economy by supporters, called neoliberal attack on worker rights by critics. Temer himself extremely unpopular (single-digit approval), accused of corruption (twice escaped prosecution due to Congressional protection). His government represented conservative and business interests, reversing some Lula-Dilma era social policies.

events.title: Lula Imprisoned and Election
events.description: Former president Lula convicted in 'Operation Car Wash' investigation of corruption and money laundering (related to beachfront apartment), sentenced 12 years imprisonment and began serving April. Conviction extremely controversial, Lula and supporters called it 'lawfare' aimed at preventing his candidacy (he leading polls then). Supreme Electoral Court banned him from running. Without Lula, Workers' Party nominated Haddad. Far-right candidate Jair Bolsonaro (former military, congressman) rose with anti-corruption, anti-PT, anti-crime, conservative values platform. Bolsonaro easily defeated Haddad in second round, exploiting anti-PT sentiment, economic discontent, social media and fake news campaign. 2018 election marked Brazil's sharp right turn and further democratic polarization.

events.title: Bolsonaro Presidency
events.description: Jair Bolsonaro served as president, promoting far-right agenda: free market reforms (pension reform, privatization), relaxing environmental protections, encouraging Amazon development, gun rights, opposing 'cultural Marxism,' attacking media and opposition. His rhetoric often provoked controversy (race, gender, human rights). During 2020 COVID-19 pandemic, Bolsonaro downplayed virus (called 'little flu'), opposed lockdowns and masks, promoted unproven treatments, clashed with governors, delayed vaccine procurement. Brazil became one of worst pandemic countries (over 700000 deaths). Amazon deforestation surged, environmental departments weakened. Bolsonaro established alliances with Trump and populist right internationally. Government riddled with scandals (fake news networks, vaccine procurement corruption).

events.title: Lula Conviction Annulled
events.description: Supreme Court ruled Curitiba judge Sérgio Moro (judge who convicted Lula, later became Bolsonaro's Justice Minister) biased, annulled Lula's conviction. This restored Lula's political rights, allowing him to run for office. Moro and 'Operation Car Wash' legitimacy questioned (exposing their improper collusion with prosecutors). Lula released and resumed political activities, preparing for 2022 election competition. He still faced other cases, but no longer convicted.

events.title: Lula Re-elected President
events.description: In extremely polarized election, 79-year-old Lula narrowly defeated incumbent Bolsonaro (50.9% vs 49.1%), achieving political comeback. Lula formed broad coalition (from left to center-right) against Bolsonaro. Campaign focused on democracy, economy (inflation, unemployment), environment and pandemic handling. Bolsonaro performed unexpectedly strong in backward regions, showing Brazil's deep social divisions. Bolsonaro didn't clearly concede defeat, supporters questioned election results (without evidence). Lula's victory viewed as democracy rescue and Brazil's left turn, but he faced enormous challenges: repairing economy, reducing inequality, protecting environment, healing divided nation.

events.title: Lula Third Term and Challenges
events.description: Lula's third term (first year) faces deeply divided nation, difficult economy (high interest rates, debt, inflation), hostile Congress and judicial system independence. His priorities include: restoring social programs (expanding Bolsa Família), raising minimum wage, combating Amazon deforestation (achieving some success, deforestation rate declining), rebuilding environmental agencies, restoring Brazil's international reputation (participating in climate negotiations, mediating Russia-Ukraine war). But limited fiscal space, reform agenda (tax reform) blocked in Congress. Lula also faces continued resistance from Bolsonarismo movement. Brazil remains Latin America's largest economy and democracy, but faces structural challenges: inequality, violence, corruption, political polarization, environmental destruction. Lula's success will determine Brazil's future direction: whether restoring inclusive development and democratic consolidation, or continuing polarization and instability. 2024 Brazil hosted G20 summit, showing its continued global importance, though domestic challenges enormous.

events.title: Brasília Capitol Riots
events.description: One week after Lula inauguration, thousands Bolsonaro supporters (incited by election fraud conspiracy theories) attacked and occupied Brasília's Congress, Presidential Palace and Supreme Court buildings, vandalizing interior facilities and artworks. This compared to January 6 2021 US Capitol riot. Security forces eventually dispersed mob, arresting over 1500 people. Event shocked Brazil and world, highlighting democratic fragility and polarization dangers. Government and judiciary took action prosecuting participants and instigators (including investigating Bolsonaro's possible role). Riots became shameful final chapter of Bolsonaro era legacy, highlighting challenges facing Lula government.
